title: How Safecracking Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant discuss safe cracking, opening with banter about movies featuring safe cracking (Sexy Beast, Bad Santa, Die Hard, Out of Sight) and Josh's thumb injury. They cover the difference between fire safes and burglary safes, how combination locks work (wheels, notches, fence, lever), legal issues around safe cracking as a separate crime, professional safe technicians, Harry Miller and other famous safe crackers, default and daylocked combinations, sticky-note combinations, lock manipulation (listening and graphing to find wheel numbers), drilling with cobalt plates, boroscopes, relockers, phosgene gas vials, torches and plasma cutters, nitroglycerin "jam shots," and electronic safe locks cracked via UV ink. The episode closes with a listener mail question from Julia about life after college and quarter-life crises.

segments.title: Opening banter and favorite safe cracking movies
segments.summary: Josh describes his thumb injury and the hosts chat about favorite safe-cracking movies such as Sexy Beast, Bad Santa, Die Hard and Out of Sight.

segments.title: Safe vulnerabilities and fire vs burglary safes
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why no safe is truly uncrackable, the types of home safes (fire safes, media safes, gun safes, burglary safes), and how fire and burglary ratings differ.

segments.title: How combination locks work
segments.summary: Explanation of group one and group two combination locks, wheels, notches, the fence, and the lever and bolt mechanism, noting the design dates back about a hundred years.

segments.title: Safe cracking as a crime and professional safe technicians
segments.summary: Safe cracking is a separate charge from burglary and larceny, and a notable case about a long sentence for safe cracking was taken to the Supreme Court. Safe technicians open safes legitimately for clients.

segments.title: Harry Miller and famous safe crackers
segments.summary: Harry C. Miller, known as Miller the Safe Man, is described for his career, his manipulation-proof lock, and a Kentucky lock museum. Jeff Star and Charlie Santory are also mentioned.

segments.title: Default combinations, daylocking and sticky notes
segments.summary: Simple methods include trying default factory combinations, opening a safe that was left daylocked, and finding a written combination nearby.

segments.title: Lock manipulation
segments.summary: Lock manipulation opens a safe by sight and sound without drilling. It involves graphing lever positions over many attempts, narrowing to candidate numbers, and trying their orders. Harry Miller could do it in about twenty minutes. Movie versions are unrealistically fast.

segments.title: Drilling safes, relockers and gas traps
segments.summary: Drilling through cobalt plates with diamond or tungsten carbide bits, using a boroscope or arthroscope to view the mechanism, relockers that trip when glass is breached, and old phosgene gas vials as a trap.

segments.title: Torches, plasma cutters and nitroglycerin
segments.summary: Oxy-acetylene torches, thermic lances and plasma cutters are discussed as cutting methods. Research on the target and the jam shot using nitroglycerin to blow off a safe door are also covered.

segments.title: Electronic safes and UV ink attack
segments.summary: Electronic locks allow many combinations and app access. A thief can use ultraviolet ink on a keypad and a black light to find the pressed numbers. The hosts then discuss what people store in home safes.
topics: what to store in a fire safe

segments.title: Listener mail: Julia's question about life after college
segments.summary: Julia asks about the hosts' jobs after college and whether they felt lost. The hosts describe their path to How Stuff Works and advise not to stress about quarter-life crises.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank Julia and invite listeners to get in touch through the website and email.
